full_judgment:
2.  Facts of the case are that the appellant-company claim to be owner in possession of the Ramgarh Tea Estate situated at naiad within P.S. Fatikchari in the District of Chittagong. In settlement case Nos. 115, 117 and 186 of 1942-43. Kbila land measuring 625. 74 acres appertaining to Khatian No. 1/16 of Mouza Ramgarh within P.S. Fatikchari was settled with the appertaining company's Ramgarh Tea Estate with effect from April 1, 1945. Upon ,receipt of Rs. 2504 as Salami and Rs. 62600 as rent for one year from the appellant-company receipt, Dakbilas were granted by the Government to it which also got possession of the land. A sum of Rs. 206500 as determiner the Divisional Forest Officer for the standing forest was also realized from the appellant company which has since then been in peaceful possession of the land after reclaiming and improving the same at a huge cost. In 1969 the management of the Ramgarh Tea Estate was taken over by the Government of Pakistan under memo No. 7(162)-Board/69 dated 4-12-69 as an enemy property. After liberation of the country the management of the Tea Estate was transferred to Bangladesh Tea Board under notification No. Sec-IA/2M-58/71-pt/118- Cord dated 1-3-72. The Government, however, subsequently released the Tea Estate in favors of the appellant-company under memo No. IM-53/74-Exp-1/539/1(8) dated 21-12-74 and since the handing over of the possession on February 1, 1975 the appellant company claims to have been managing the Tea Estate including the land as well. 

 3. Meanwhile, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Chittagong by his order dated June 3, 1973 declared the aforesaid land as abandoned land under Section 92 (1C) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. A Miscellaneous Case No. 2/72-73 was filed by the appellant-company claiming that the land in question was leased out to it who have been possessing the same on payment of rent. The appellant-company also moved the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh. The objections were, however, not entertained by the respondents. The appellant-company then moved the High Court under Article 102 of the Constitution challenging the impugned order on the ground that Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act did not apply to the facts of the case. The respondents, namely, the Government of Bangladesh, the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong and the Circle Officer, Fatikchari entered appearance by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. It was contended by them that the land in dispute was settled with one Hiralal Mukherjee, Manager of the Tea Estate, in his personal capacity and not as manager of the Tea Estate. Further, in 1950 Hiralal Mukherjee relinquished all his claims to the land in favour of a different parson namely, M/s. Union Agency Ltd. under a registered deed of relinquishment. A mutation case, being case No. 2/1 of 1950-51, was filed by M/s. Union Agency Ltd. for recording its name as owner in possession of the land. After notices were served upon parties concerned including the appellant-company and the Manager of the Ramgarh Tea Estate all of whom supported its claim, the mutation case was allowed and M/s. Union Agency Ltd. was recorded as tenant. After mutation the land was recorded as Jote No. 164 under a separate Khatian No. 1/36. Since Union Agency Ltd. left the country without making any arrangement for payment of rent the land became abandoned under Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and was rightly declared to be so by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Chittagong. 

 6. Mr. S.R. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, submitted that the earned Judges of the High Court were wrong in deciding the disputed question of facts relating to title to the land which could only have been done by taking proper evidence, oral and documentary Whether the relinquishment by Hirala Mukherjee, Manager of Ramgarh Tea Estate in whose favour the land was originally settled regally transferred title in favour of the Union Agency Ltd. depended on the decision as to whether a registered document was necessary to effect the relinquishment. The learned Counsel also submitted that the decision as to whether the Union Agency Ltd. was a part and parcel of the appellant-company required investigation into facts. It appears that the High Court did not believe the genuineness of the rent receipt dated 25.3.67 produced by the appellant-company in support of its claim that rent was being paid by the company to the Government and it also found discrepancies with respect to the Khatian number mentioned in the rent receipt. The land in dispute was recorded as Khatian No. 1/36 after the mutation case No. 2/1, whereas the rent receipt showed that rent was being paid in respect of land in Khatian No. 1/38. Further, there was no reason as to why the appellant-company whose name was not recorded in the Khatian should pay rent in respect of the land of which M/c. Union Agency Ltd. was the recorded tenant, The questions raised by the learned Counsel relate to the title of the appellant-company which depend on facts which are in dispute and can only be settled after full evidence has been properly taken. Mr. Sultan Hossain the learned Deputy Attorney General who appeared on be If of the Government also conceded that where facts are disputed; the high Court, in exercising jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution not proceed to settle the disputed facts requiring taking of evidence. There is a long line of decisions in favour of the view that the High Court should not enter in to disputed questions of fact nor decide any question as to title which require investigation into facts and taking of elaborate evidence.
